```{r setup-module1, context="setup", include=FALSE}
library(learnr)
library(shiny)
library(DBI)
library(RPostgres)
library(bslib)
library(shinychat)
library(ellmer)
library(promises)

# Shared database helper functions (get_con, get_or_create_student,
# get_exercise_id, log_attempt, log_chat, get_student_progress)
source("R/db_utils.R")
# Tutor chat context assembly, start_tutor_chat(), the shared
# bs5_theme_dependencies()/wire_tutor_chat()/log_attempt_and_maybe_open_chat()
# wiring, and the quiz_question_ui()/quiz_question_server() helpers used
# below in place of learnr::question() -- see their definitions in
# R/tutor_utils.R for why.
source("R/tutor_utils.R")

# Grading logic for this module's one exercise. Unchanged from the
# gradethis-based version -- only how it's *called* changed (see the
# "Wrapping up" topic below), not the grading logic itself.
evaluate_name_exercise <- function(result, stage) {
  passed <- TRUE
  feedback_message <- "Nice -- that's exactly right! Your response has been recorded."

  if (is.null(result) || !is.character(result) || nchar(trimws(result)) == 0) {
    passed <- FALSE
    feedback_message <- if (identical(stage, "error_check")) {
      "That code doesn't run as-is -- check that your name is wrapped in matching quotation marks."
    } else {
      "Make sure to type your name inside quotation marks."
    }
  } else if (identical(trimws(result), "___")) {
    passed <- FALSE
    feedback_message <- "Looks like the placeholder is still there -- replace `___` with your own name."
  }

  list(passed = passed, message = feedback_message)
}
```

```{r, context="server"}
# --- Identity capture -------------------------------------------------
# Every tutorial session starts by asking for a name. This is a
# deliberately simple stand-in for real identity -- no roster/Canvas
# matching yet. The resulting student_id is stored on session$userData,
# which is the safe, session-scoped place to keep it so that exercise
# checking code (which runs in a more isolated context) can still reach
# it via shiny::getDefaultReactiveDomain().
#
# Also computes the "welcome back" progress banner (below, in the Module 1
# Welcome topic) for a returning student -- see get_student_progress() in
# R/db_utils.R. A brand-new student (0 exercises passed) sees no banner.

# Active-time logging for the instructor dashboard -- see
# activity_tracker_ui()/activity_tracker_server() in R/tutor_utils.R.
activity_tracker_server(input, session)

# Progress gating -- quizzes/exercises must be finished before moving on.
# Must run before any quiz_question_server()/exercise_server() call so they
# can register. See gating_ui()/gating_server() in R/tutor_utils.R.
gating_server(input, session)

showModal(modalDialog(
  title = "Welcome!",
  "Please enter your name to begin this tutorial.",
  textInput("student_name", label = NULL, placeholder = "Your name"),
  footer = actionButton("submit_name", "Start Tutorial"),
  easyClose = FALSE
))

observeEvent(input$submit_name, {
  req(input$student_name)
  tryCatch({
    con <- get_con()
    sid <- get_or_create_student(con, trimws(input$student_name))
    progress <- get_student_progress(con, sid)
    gate_load_student(session, con, sid)
    dbDisconnect(con)

    session$userData$student_id <- sid
    removeModal()

    if (progress$exercises_passed > 0) {
      output$welcome_back_banner <- renderUI({
        message_text <- if (is.na(progress$next_module_title)) {
          sprintf(
            "Welcome back! You've completed all %d exercises -- great work!",
            progress$total_exercises
          )
        } else {
          sprintf(
            "Welcome back! You've completed %d of %d exercises. Pick up in %s using the sidebar on the left.",
            progress$exercises_passed, progress$total_exercises, progress$next_module_title
          )
        }
        tags$div(class = "alert alert-info", message_text)
      })
    }
  }, error = function(e) {
    showModal(modalDialog(
      title = "Couldn't connect",
      paste("There was a problem saving your name (database error):", conditionMessage(e)),
      footer = actionButton("submit_name", "Try again"),
      easyClose = FALSE
    ))
  })
})
```

```{r, context="server"}
# --- "Quick system check" exercise ---------------------------------------
# Plain Shiny replacement for the gradethis exercise=TRUE chunk (same
# client-side interaction-binding issue as the quizzes above). A plain
# textAreaInput() stands in for the ace.js code editor learnr normally
# provides -- a deliberate simplification for this trivial one-line
# exercise, not a general-purpose code editor replacement.

gate_register_exercise(session, "name_exercise", "module1_name_check", "tutor_accordion_m1_1")

observeEvent(input$name_exercise_reset, {
  updateTextAreaInput(session, "name_exercise_code", value = '"___"')
  output$name_exercise_feedback <- renderUI(NULL)
})

observeEvent(input$name_exercise_submit, {
  user_code <- input$name_exercise_code
  parsed_result <- tryCatch(eval(parse(text = user_code)), error = function(e) e)
  is_error <- inherits(parsed_result, "error")
  stage <- if (is_error) "error_check" else "check"
  eval_result <- evaluate_name_exercise(if (is_error) NULL else parsed_result, stage)

  student_id <- session$userData$student_id
  log_attempt_and_maybe_open_chat(
    "module1_name_check", student_id, user_code,
    eval_result$passed, eval_result$message, "tutor_accordion_m1_1", session
  )
  if (eval_result$passed) gate_complete(session, "name_exercise") else gate_record_fail(session, "name_exercise")

  output$name_exercise_feedback <- renderUI({
    tagList(
      tags$pre(if (is_error) {
        paste("Error:", conditionMessage(parsed_result))
      } else {
        paste(utils::capture.output(print(parsed_result)), collapse = "\n")
      }),
      tags$div(
        class = if (eval_result$passed) "alert alert-success" else "alert alert-danger",
        eval_result$message
      )
    )
  })
})
```

This course gets you ready to use R in the rest of the class. The goal isn't to make you a programmer -- most of the code you'll work with later will come from your instructor or an AI assistant. The goal is that you can **run that code, read what it tells you, and catch it when it's wrong**.

Go through the modules in order. Everything is explained from the beginning, and nothing assumes you've seen code before.

How it works:

- **Quizzes** ask you to predict what code will do. Answer before you scroll back up to check -- the first try is the one that tells you whether you've got it.
- **Exercises** have you write, fix, or finish real R code, and check it when you click **Submit Answer**. Submit as often as you like.
- **The course opens up as you go.** Each quiz needs a correct answer and each exercise needs to pass before the next part appears. If an exercise has you truly stuck, the course will let you move on after several honest tries.
- **Ask the Tutor** sits under every exercise. It's an AI tutor that sees your latest attempt -- use it whenever you're stuck *or* curious, before or after submitting. It will help you get there rather than hand you the answer.

Nothing in this module involves writing R code yet -- that starts in Module 2.

## Module 1: Installing R and RStudio

R and RStudio are two different pieces of software that work together:

- **R** is the actual programming language -- the engine that runs your code.
- **RStudio** is an *interface* for working with R more comfortably -- it doesn't replace R, it sits on top of it.

You install them in that order: R first (from CRAN), then RStudio (from posit.co), since RStudio needs an existing R installation to attach to.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
quiz_question_ui("install_quiz", "Which of these is true about the relationship between R and RStudio?", c(
  "RStudio replaces R -- you only need to install RStudio." = "wrong_replaces",
  "R is the language/engine, and RStudio is an interface built on top of it." = "correct",
  "R and RStudio are two unrelated tools with no connection." = "wrong_unrelated"
))
```

This tutorial runs entirely in your browser, so it has no way to see your own computer or confirm your install actually worked -- the steps below are the real, click-by-click process, but you're doing them in a separate window, alongside this one. Keep both open side by side if you can.

Installation is the one part of this course that depends on your specific computer, so if something doesn't match what's described below, ask here rather than getting stuck.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
accordion(
  id = "tutor_accordion_m1_install",
  open = FALSE,
  accordion_panel(
    title = "Ask the Tutor",
    chat_ui(
      "tutor_chat_m1_install",
      placeholder = "Ask about an installation problem...",
      greeting = INSTALL_HELP_CHAT_GREETING,
      allow_attachments = FALSE
    )
  )
)
```

### Step 1: Install R

<details>
<summary><strong>Already have R and RStudio?</strong> Check your version first.</summary>

Open RStudio and type `R.version.string` in the Console, then press Enter. If it shows a version **older than 4.1.0**, install the current R anyway using the steps below -- this course uses features (like the `|>` pipe in Module 4) that older versions don't have, and code written by AI assistants usually assumes a recent version too. If you're on 4.1.0 or newer, skip ahead to "The RStudio panes."

</details>

1. Go to **[cran.r-project.org](https://cran.r-project.org)** -- this is CRAN, the official source for R. (Don't search for "R" in a general search engine first -- it's a one-letter name and the results are mostly noise. Go straight to CRAN.)
2. Near the top, click the download link for your operating system -- **Download R for Windows**, **macOS**, or **Linux**.
3. **Windows:** click **base**, then click the large **Download R-4.x.x for Windows** link. Run the downloaded `.exe` file, and click through the installer -- **Next**, **Next**, **Install**, **Finish** -- accepting every default option. You don't need to change anything.
4. **Mac:** you'll see two `.pkg` links, one for **Apple silicon (arm64)** and one for **Intel (x86_64)**. If you're not sure which chip your Mac has, check the Apple menu (top-left) > **About This Mac**. Download the matching one, open it, and follow the installer, accepting the defaults.

That's it for this step -- once the installer finishes, R itself is installed, but you won't see any new icon to click yet. That's expected; R on its own has no visible interface. That's exactly what RStudio is for, which is the next step.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
quiz_question_ui("install_r_quiz", "You've just downloaded the R installer file (the .exe or .pkg). What should you do with it?", c(
  "Delete it -- you don't need it once it's downloaded." = "wrong_delete",
  "Open/run it and click through the installation wizard, accepting the defaults." = "correct",
  "Rename it to \"RStudio\" so it opens the right program." = "wrong_rename"
))
```

### Step 2: Install RStudio

1. Go to **[posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/)**.
2. That page actually lists installing R as its own "Step 1" (which you already did above) -- scroll down to **Step 2: Install RStudio**.
3. Click the download button for the free **RStudio Desktop** version matching your operating system.
4. Run the installer and, same as before, click through it accepting the defaults.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
quiz_question_ui("install_rstudio_quiz", "Suppose you skipped installing R and only installed RStudio. What would happen when you tried to open RStudio?", c(
  "It would work exactly the same -- RStudio doesn't actually need R." = "wrong_same",
  "It would either fail to open properly or prompt you that no R installation was found." = "correct",
  "It would automatically download and install R for you first." = "wrong_autoinstall"
))
```

### Step 3: Open RStudio and do a first check

Open **RStudio** now -- not R by itself; look for the RStudio icon specifically, since installing R doesn't create a separate icon for it, and R itself has no real interface to open.

The first time it launches, RStudio automatically detects the R installation from Step 1 -- you shouldn't need to point it at anything manually. You'll see a window split into a few panes (covered in detail in the next section); for now, find the **Console** pane -- it's the one with a `>` prompt waiting for input.

Click into the Console, type:

```
2 + 2
```

and press **Enter**. You should see:

```
[1] 4
```

That confirms R and RStudio are both installed and talking to each other correctly.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
quiz_question_ui("first_check_quiz", "You open RStudio, type 2 + 2 in the Console, and press Enter -- but instead of [1] 4, you get an error like \"R version not found\" or the Console looks broken. What's the most likely explanation?", c(
  "RStudio is broken and needs to be reinstalled." = "wrong_broken",
  "R wasn't fully installed (or installed correctly) in Step 1 -- go back and reinstall R, then reopen RStudio." = "correct",
  "You need to install a separate \"math package\" before RStudio can do arithmetic." = "wrong_mathpkg"
))
```

## Module 1: The RStudio panes

When you open RStudio, you'll typically see four panes:

- **Source** (top-left) -- where you write and edit scripts
- **Console** (bottom-left) -- where code actually runs, one command at a time
- **Environment / History** (top-right) -- shows the objects you've created and what you've run
- **Files / Plots / Packages / Help** (bottom-right) -- a multi-purpose pane for browsing files, viewing plots, managing packages, and reading documentation

```{r, echo=FALSE}
quiz_question_ui("panes_quiz", "If you want to see a plot you just created, which pane would you look at?", c(
  "Source" = "wrong_source",
  "Console" = "wrong_console",
  "Environment / History" = "wrong_env",
  "Files / Plots / Packages / Help" = "correct"
))
```

## Module 1: Working directory

Your **working directory** is the folder R treats as "home base." When code names a file, like `read.csv("birds.csv")`, R looks for it starting from that folder. `getwd()` ("get working directory") prints which folder that is.

A file path *without* a drive letter at the front is **relative**: it starts from the working directory. So if the working directory is `C:/Users/sam/Documents`, then `"data/birds.csv"` means `C:/Users/sam/Documents/data/birds.csv`.

The most reliable way to manage this is an **RStudio Project** (File > New Project): a folder with a `.Rproj` file in it. Opening the project sets the working directory to that folder automatically, so the same relative paths work every time -- on your computer and on anyone else's.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
quiz_question_ui("wd_quiz", "getwd() prints \"C:/Users/sam/Documents\". Your file is at C:/Users/sam/Documents/project/data/birds.csv. Which line reads it?", c(
  "read.csv(\"birds.csv\")" = "wrong_name",
  "read.csv(\"data/birds.csv\")" = "wrong_partial",
  "read.csv(\"project/data/birds.csv\")" = "correct",
  "read.csv(\"C:/Users/sam/Documents\")" = "wrong_folder"
))
```

### Up next

Module 2 introduces actual R code -- installing packages, reading the console, and running provided scripts.

```{r setup-module2, context="setup", include=FALSE}
# Grading logic for this module's exercises. See R/tutor_utils.R for the
# shared exercise/tutor wiring.

evaluate_comment_exercise <- function(user_code, result, stage) {
  test_line_commented <- grepl("(?m)^\\s*#.*temps\\s*\\*\\s*2", user_code, perl = TRUE)
  test_line_active <- grepl("(?m)^\\s*temps\\s*<-\\s*temps\\s*\\*\\s*2", user_code, perl = TRUE)
  first_line_active <- grepl("(?m)^\\s*temps\\s*<-\\s*c\\(", user_code, perl = TRUE)
  correct_result <- is.numeric(result) && length(result) == 1 && isTRUE(all.equal(result, mean(c(18, 21, 25))))

  passed <- test_line_commented && !test_line_active && first_line_active && correct_result

  feedback_message <- if (passed) {
    "Right -- the leftover test line is switched off, so the mean is back to the real 21.33."
  } else if (identical(stage, "error_check")) {
    "That code doesn't run as-is now -- make sure you only added a # at the start of one line, without changing anything else."
  } else if (!first_line_active) {
    "The first line (creating temps) needs to stay active -- without it there's nothing to average."
  } else if (test_line_active) {
    "The result is still doubled -- which line is changing temps after it's created? Put a # at the very start of that line."
  } else if (!test_line_commented) {
    "Comment that line out with # rather than deleting it -- the point is being able to switch it back on later."
  } else {
    "Close -- the last line should still print the mean of temps."
  }

  list(passed = passed, message = feedback_message)
}

evaluate_fix_the_bug_exercise <- function(user_code, result, stage) {
  passed <- !is.null(result) && is.character(result) && identical(trimws(result), "Hello")
  still_misspelled <- grepl("pritn", user_code, fixed = TRUE)

  feedback_message <- if (passed) {
    "Fixed -- both problems. Notice R only reported one at a time: fixing an error often uncovers the next one."
  } else if (identical(stage, "error_check") && still_misspelled) {
    "Read the error: R can't find a function with that name. Look closely at how the function's name is spelled."
  } else if (identical(stage, "error_check")) {
    "One down! Now R is looking for an object called Hello. Is Hello meant to be the name of something, or text?"
  } else {
    "The code runs, but it should print the word Hello. Double check what you changed."
  }

  list(passed = passed, message = feedback_message)
}
```

```{r, context="server"}
# --- Quiz question wiring ------------------------------------------------
# "What would happen / what does this mean" questions built around
# situations students actually hit -- especially when running code someone
# else (or an AI) wrote.
quiz_question_server(input, output, session, "packages_quiz", module_number = 2, list(
  correct = list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct! \"There is no package called...\" means it's not installed on this computer yet. Install it once, then library() works."),
  wrong_quotes = list(correct = FALSE, message = "library() accepts the name with or without quotes -- that's not the problem. The message says the package isn't on this computer at all."),
  wrong_update = list(correct = FALSE, message = "update.packages() only updates packages you already have -- this one was never installed."),
  wrong_restart = list(correct = FALSE, message = "Restarting won't help: the package isn't on this computer, so there's nothing to load.")
))

quiz_question_server(input, output, session, "console_quiz", module_number = 2, list(
  correct = list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct! + means R thinks the command isn't finished -- usually a missing ) or \". Finish it, or press Esc to cancel and start over."),
  wrong_add = list(correct = FALSE, message = "The + here isn't addition -- it's the Console's prompt changing from > to +, which means R is waiting for more."),
  wrong_crash = list(correct = FALSE, message = "R is fine -- it's just waiting for you to finish the command you started.")
))

quiz_question_server(input, output, session, "running_quiz", module_number = 2, list(
  correct = list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct! R only knows what you've actually run in this session -- not what's written in the file. Run line 1 first (or run the whole script)."),
  wrong_typo = list(correct = FALSE, message = "Both lines spell temps the same way. The problem is which lines have actually been run."),
  wrong_package = list(correct = FALSE, message = "mean() is built into R -- no package needed. Look at what R says it can't find."),
  wrong_corrupt = list(correct = FALSE, message = "Nothing's wrong with the file -- R just hasn't run line 1 yet in this session.")
))

quiz_question_server(input, output, session, "warning_quiz", module_number = 2, list(
  correct = list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct! A warning means the code ran, but something may not be what you expect. Here \"n/a\" silently became NA -- easy to miss if you skip warnings."),
  wrong_ignore = list(correct = FALSE, message = "Warnings are often the only sign a result is quietly wrong. This one is telling you a value turned into NA."),
  wrong_failed = list(correct = FALSE, message = "It didn't fail -- you got a result: 12 15 NA. That's what makes warnings easy to ignore."),
  wrong_fixed = list(correct = FALSE, message = "R didn't fix anything -- it replaced \"n/a\" with NA (missing) and warned you that it did.")
))

quiz_question_server(input, output, session, "help_quiz", module_number = 2, list(
  correct = list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct! digits = 0 is a default: if you don't give digits, round() uses 0 -- whole numbers."),
  wrong_257 = list(correct = FALSE, message = "That would need digits = 2. The Usage line shows what happens when you leave digits out."),
  wrong_error = list(correct = FALSE, message = "An argument written as name = value in Usage has a default, so you can leave it out."),
  wrong_25 = list(correct = FALSE, message = "Rounding to whole numbers turns 2.567 into 3, not 2.5.")
))
```

## Module 2: Welcome back

This module is where you start touching code: packages, the Console, comments, running code someone else wrote, and -- probably most useful of all -- reading what R tells you when something goes wrong.

You are **not** expected to write much code from scratch in this course. You *are* expected to run code you're handed, notice when it's misbehaving, and fix it.

<details>
<summary><strong>New to code?</strong> Two words you'll see constantly.</summary>

A **function** is a named command that does one job, written with parentheses after its name: `mean(x)`, `print("hi")`, `library(dplyr)`. What goes inside the parentheses are its **arguments** -- the inputs you hand it. Some arguments have names, like `digits` in `round(3.14159, digits = 2)`.

</details>

## Module 2: Packages

Most real work uses **packages**: bundles of extra functions other people wrote. Using one takes two steps:

1. **`install.packages("dplyr")`** downloads it onto your computer. Once per computer.
2. **`library(dplyr)`** loads it into your current session. Every time you start R and want to use it.

Code you're handed -- especially from an AI -- usually starts with `library()` lines and assumes the packages are already installed.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
quiz_question_ui("packages_quiz", "You run library(janitor) and get: Error in library(janitor) : there is no package called 'janitor'. What do you run?", c(
  "install.packages(\"janitor\"), then library(janitor) again" = "correct",
  "library(\"janitor\") -- with quotes this time" = "wrong_quotes",
  "update.packages()" = "wrong_update",
  "Nothing -- just restart RStudio and try again" = "wrong_restart"
))
```

## Module 2: The Console

The **Console** runs code the moment you press Enter. A `>` prompt means R is ready for the next command. It's great for quick checks, but nothing typed there is saved -- real work goes in a **script** (a `.R` file) that you can save, edit, and re-run.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
quiz_question_ui("console_quiz", "You press Enter and the Console shows + instead of >. What does that mean?", c(
  "R is waiting for you to finish the command -- usually a missing ) or quotation mark" = "correct",
  "R added the numbers you typed" = "wrong_add",
  "R crashed and needs to be restarted" = "wrong_crash"
))
```

## Module 2: Comments

Anything after a `#` on a line is a **comment**, and R ignores it. Comments are for two things:

- **Notes** explaining *why* code does something.
- **Switching a line off** without deleting it -- extremely common when testing: comment a line out, see what changes, switch it back on later.

### Practice: switch off a leftover line

This should report the average of the three temperatures (about 21.3), but someone left a test line in that changes them. Find it and comment it out -- don't delete it.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
exercise_ui("comment_exercise", "temps <- c(18, 21, 25)\ntemps <- temps * 2   # quick test -- remove later\nmean(temps)")
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
accordion(
  id = "tutor_accordion_m2_1",
  open = FALSE,
  accordion_panel(
    title = "Ask the Tutor",
    chat_ui(
      "tutor_chat_m2_1",
      placeholder = "Ask a question about this exercise...",
      greeting = TUTOR_CHAT_GREETING,
      allow_attachments = FALSE
    )
  )
)
```

## Module 2: Running code someone gives you

Much of the code you'll use comes from your instructor or an AI assistant -- running it is a normal, professional way to work. In RStudio:

- **Ctrl+Enter** (Cmd+Return on Mac) runs the line your cursor is on, then moves to the next line.
- **Source** (Ctrl+Shift+Enter) runs the whole file, top to bottom.

R only knows about what you've actually *run* in this session -- not what's written in the file.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
quiz_question_ui("running_quiz", "A script's line 1 is temps <- c(18, 21, 25) and line 2 is mean(temps). You open it fresh, click on line 2, press Ctrl+Enter, and get: object 'temps' not found. Why?", c(
  "Line 1 hasn't been run in this session yet" = "correct",
  "temps is spelled differently on the two lines" = "wrong_typo",
  "mean() needs a package loaded first" = "wrong_package",
  "The script file is corrupted" = "wrong_corrupt"
))
```

## Module 2: Errors and warnings

Red text isn't a sign you've broken something. It's R telling you, often quite specifically, what it couldn't do:

- **`object 'x' not found`** -- R has no object called `x`. Usually a typo, a line that hasn't been run, or text that's missing its quotation marks.
- **`could not find function "f"`** -- a misspelled function name, or a package that hasn't been loaded with `library()`.
- **`unexpected symbol` / `unexpected ')'`** -- a syntax slip: a missing comma, parenthesis, or quotation mark.

Unquoted words are treated as *names*: `print(Hello)` looks for an object called `Hello`, while `print("Hello")` prints the text.

A **warning** is different from an error: the code *ran* and gave you a result, but R is flagging something you should check. Warnings are easy to ignore, and they're often the only sign a result is quietly wrong.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
quiz_question_ui("warning_quiz", "You run as.numeric(c(\"12\", \"15\", \"n/a\")) and get [1] 12 15 NA, plus: Warning message: NAs introduced by coercion. What does the warning mean?", c(
  "It ran, but \"n/a\" couldn't become a number, so it's now NA -- check before using the result" = "correct",
  "Nothing important -- warnings can be ignored" = "wrong_ignore",
  "The code failed and produced no result" = "wrong_failed",
  "R fixed the problem automatically" = "wrong_fixed"
))
```

### Practice: fix the errors

This should print the word `Hello`. It has two problems, and R will only tell you about one at a time -- read each message, fix that, run it again.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
exercise_ui("fix_the_bug_exercise", "pritn(Hello)")
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
  id = "tutor_accordion_m2_2",
  open = FALSE,
  accordion_panel(
    title = "Ask the Tutor",
    chat_ui(
      "tutor_chat_m2_2",
      placeholder = "Ask a question about this exercise...",
      greeting = TUTOR_CHAT_GREETING,
      allow_attachments = FALSE
    )
  )
)
```

## Module 2: Getting help

Every function has a help page: run **`?round`** (or `help(round)`) and it opens in the Help pane. The most useful part is **Usage**, which shows the arguments and their defaults. An argument written as `name = value` has a default, so you can leave it out:

```
round(x, digits = 0)
```

An AI assistant can answer the same questions, but `?` is always available, works offline, and comes straight from the package's authors -- useful for checking what an AI told you.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
quiz_question_ui("help_quiz", "Based on that Usage line, what does round(2.567) return?", c(
  "3" = "correct",
  "2.57" = "wrong_257",
  "An error, because digits wasn't given" = "wrong_error",
  "2.5" = "wrong_25"
))
```

## Module 2: Wrapping up

**If you remember only a few things from this module:**

- Read the error message -- it usually says exactly what R couldn't find or understand. Fixing one error can uncover the next; that's normal.
- A warning means the code ran but something may be off. Don't skip it.
- R only knows what you've run, in the order you ran it -- not what's sitting in your script.
- Install a package once per computer; `library()` it every session.

### Up next

Module 3 gets into actual data: data types, vectors, comparisons, and turning a formula into code.

```{r setup-module3, context="setup", include=FALSE}
# Grading logic for this module's exercises. See R/tutor_utils.R for the
# shared exercise/tutor wiring.

# Given input for the "Turning a formula into code" exercise. Like Module
# 4's fish_clean, it has to be placed in globalenv() explicitly:
# exercise_server()'s eval(parse(text = user_code), envir = new.env())
# resolves its parent chain through globalenv(), not through this setup
# chunk's own local environment.
temps_f <- c(32, 212, 98.6)
assign("temps_f", temps_f, envir = globalenv())

evaluate_assignment_exercise <- function(user_code, result, envir, stage) {
  price_ok <- !is.null(envir) && exists("price", envir = envir, inherits = FALSE) && isTRUE(get("price", envir = envir) == 5)
  qty_ok <- !is.null(envir) && exists("qty", envir = envir, inherits = FALSE) && isTRUE(get("qty", envir = envir) == 3)
  typed_answer <- grepl("15", user_code, fixed = TRUE)
  correct_result <- is.numeric(result) && length(result) == 1 && isTRUE(result == 15)

  passed <- price_ok && qty_ok && !typed_answer && correct_result

  feedback_message <- if (passed) {
    "Right -- total has to be recalculated after price changes. A variable stores a value, not a formula."
  } else if (identical(stage, "error_check")) {
    "That code doesn't run as-is -- check that every line is a complete assignment or expression."
  } else if (typed_answer) {
    "Don't type 15 yourself -- the point is getting R to calculate it from price and qty, so it stays right if they change again."
  } else if (!price_ok || !qty_ok) {
    "Keep price as 5 and qty as 3 -- the fix is about when total gets calculated, not the inputs."
  } else if (is.numeric(result) && isTRUE(result == 12)) {
    "Still 12. total was calculated back when price was 4, and it doesn't update itself. What has to happen after price changes?"
  } else {
    "Not 15 yet -- total should be the new price times qty."
  }

  list(passed = passed, message = feedback_message)
}

evaluate_vectors_exercise <- function(user_code, result, stage) {
  uses_index <- grepl("scores\\s*\\[", user_code)
  typed_values <- grepl("c\\(\\s*20\\s*,\\s*40\\s*\\)", user_code)
  correct_result <- is.numeric(result) && identical(as.numeric(result), c(20, 40))

  passed <- uses_index && !typed_values && correct_result

  feedback_message <- if (passed) {
    "That's it -- a vector of positions inside the brackets pulls out several elements at once."
  } else if (identical(stage, "error_check")) {
    "That code doesn't run as-is -- check the brackets and commas."
  } else if (typed_values) {
    "Pull the values out of scores by position, rather than typing 20 and 40 yourself."
  } else if (!uses_index) {
    "Use square brackets on scores to pick out elements by position."
  } else if (is.numeric(result) && length(result) == 4) {
    "Empty brackets give you everything back -- put the positions you want inside them."
  } else if (is.numeric(result) && length(result) == 1) {
    "That's one element -- you need two at once. How do you give R more than one position inside the brackets?"
  } else {
    "Not quite the 2nd and 4th elements yet -- check which positions you're asking for."
  }

  list(passed = passed, message = feedback_message)
}

evaluate_fix_comparison_exercise <- function(user_code, result, envir, stage) {
  temps_intact <- !is.null(envir) && exists("temps", envir = envir, inherits = FALSE) &&
    isTRUE(all.equal(get("temps", envir = envir), c(72, 80, 85, 80, 79)))
  uses_comparison <- grepl("==", user_code, fixed = TRUE)
  correct_result <- is.numeric(result) && length(result) == 1 && isTRUE(result == 2)

  passed <- temps_intact && uses_comparison && correct_result

  feedback_message <- if (passed) {
    "Right -- temps == 80 gives TRUE/FALSE for each day, and sum() counts the TRUEs: 2 days."
  } else if (identical(stage, "error_check")) {
    "That code doesn't run as-is -- check the comparison line is complete."
  } else if (!temps_intact) {
    "temps isn't the original five temperatures anymore -- some line is overwriting it. A single = assigns, just like <-."
  } else if (!uses_comparison) {
    "You'll need a comparison here -- R's \"is equal to\" is ==, two equals signs."
  } else {
    "You're comparing now, but the count isn't 2 yet -- sum() of a TRUE/FALSE vector counts the TRUEs."
  }

  list(passed = passed, message = feedback_message)
}

evaluate_formula_exercise <- function(user_code, result, stage) {
  uses_given <- grepl("temps_f", user_code, fixed = TRUE)
  correct_result <- (temps_f - 32) * 5 / 9
  buggy_result <- temps_f - 32 * 5 / 9
  result_ok <- is.numeric(result) && length(result) == length(correct_result) &&
    isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(result), correct_result, tolerance = 0.001))
  still_buggy <- is.numeric(result) && length(result) == 3 && isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(result), buggy_result))

  passed <- uses_given && result_ok

  feedback_message <- if (passed) {
    "Fixed -- 0, 100, and 37. And you could prove it: 212 F really is 100 C."
  } else if (identical(stage, "error_check")) {
    "That code doesn't run as-is -- check that every ( has a matching )."
  } else if (!uses_given) {
    "Compute it from temps_f, not typed-in numbers -- the point is code that works for any temperatures."
  } else if (still_buggy) {
    "Check the middle value: 212 F should come out as 100 C, but it's 194. R does * and / before -, so what is actually being subtracted from temps_f?"
  } else {
    "Not quite -- check your answer against a value you know: 212 F is 100 C, and 32 F is 0 C."
  }

  list(passed = passed, message = feedback_message)
}

evaluate_module3_cumulative_exercise <- function(user_code, result, envir, stage) {
  has_prices <- !is.null(envir) && exists("prices", envir = envir, inherits = FALSE) &&
    is.numeric(get("prices", envir = envir)) && length(get("prices", envir = envir)) == 4
  typed_answer <- grepl("12.42", user_code, fixed = TRUE)
  correct_result <- is.numeric(result) && length(result) == 1 && isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(result), 12.42))
  adds_rate <- is.numeric(result) && length(result) == 1 && isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(result), 11.58))

  passed <- has_prices && !typed_answer && correct_result

  feedback_message <- if (passed) {
    "All three fixed -- $12.42. The last one was the dangerous kind: the code ran fine and gave a believable-looking number."
  } else if (identical(stage, "error_check") && grepl("1.25 4", user_code, fixed = TRUE)) {
    "R stopped on the prices line (\"unexpected numeric constant\") -- two of the numbers inside c() aren't separated properly."
  } else if (identical(stage, "error_check") && grepl("Tax_rate", user_code, fixed = TRUE)) {
    "One down! Now R can't find an object. Compare that name, letter by letter, with the name that was actually created."
  } else if (identical(stage, "error_check")) {
    "That still doesn't run -- read the error message and fix one thing at a time. It tells you where R got stuck."
  } else if (typed_answer) {
    "Let the code calculate the total rather than typing the answer in."
  } else if (!has_prices) {
    "prices should be a vector of 4 numbers -- check the values inside c(...)."
  } else if (adds_rate) {
    "It runs now, but $11.58 is only 8 cents more than $11.50 -- that's not 8% tax. What is total + tax_rate actually adding?"
  } else {
    "It runs, but the total isn't right yet. Sanity-check it: 8% of about $11.50 is a bit under a dollar."
  }

  list(passed = passed, message = feedback_message)
}
```

## Module 3: Welcome back

This module covers the building blocks everything else sits on: types of values, variables, vectors, and comparisons. Several exercises here hand you code that **runs without an error but gives the wrong answer** -- the hardest kind of bug to notice. The habit to build: check results against something you already know.

## Module 3: Data types

Every value in R has a **type**. The three you'll meet constantly:

- **numeric** -- numbers, like `5` or `3.14`
- **character** -- text, always in quotes, like `"hello"` or `"5"`
- **logical** -- `TRUE` or `FALSE`

`class()` tells you a value's type:

```{r class-demo, echo=TRUE}
class(5)
class("5")
class(TRUE)
```

`5` and `"5"` look alike but behave differently: you can do math with the first, not the second.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
quiz_question_ui("types_quiz", "What happens when you run \"5\" + 3?", c(
  "8" = "wrong_8",
  "\"53\"" = "wrong_53",
  "An error" = "correct",
  "NA" = "wrong_na"
))
```

## Module 3: Variables and names

**Assignment** stores a value under a name with `<-` (read it as "gets"):

```{r assignment-demo, echo=TRUE}
student_score <- 92
student_score + 3
```

Names can contain letters, numbers, `.` and `_`, but can't start with a number or contain spaces. This course uses `snake_case` (`student_score`). And names are **case-sensitive**.

<details>
<summary><strong>New to this?</strong> What a variable actually holds.</summary>

Think of `<-` as writing a value on a sticky note and labeling it. `student_score <- 92` puts 92 on a note labeled `student_score`. Later, `student_score + 3` reads the note. The note holds a *value*, not a recipe -- that turns out to matter, as the next question shows.

</details>

```{r, echo=FALSE}
quiz_question_ui("naming_quiz", "You run Score <- 90, then score + 5. What happens?", c(
  "95" = "wrong_95",
  "An error: object 'score' not found" = "correct",
  "5" = "wrong_5",
  "NA" = "wrong_na"
))
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
quiz_question_ui("assign_snapshot_quiz", "What does the last line print?  price <- 4;  qty <- 3;  total <- price * qty;  price <- 5;  total", c(
  "12" = "correct",
  "15" = "wrong_15",
  "An error" = "wrong_error",
  "5" = "wrong_5"
))
```

## Module 3: Vectors

A **vector** is a sequence of values of the same type, built with `c()` ("combine"). Square brackets pull out elements by position -- counting from **1** -- and you can ask for several positions at once:

```{r vector-demo, echo=TRUE}
heights <- c(64, 68, 71, 66)
heights[1]
heights[c(1, 3)]
heights * 2
```

That last line shows something R does everywhere: an operation on a vector applies to **every element** at once.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
quiz_question_ui("vector_na_quiz", "heights has 4 values. What does heights[5] return?", c(
  "NA" = "correct",
  "An error" = "wrong_error",
  "66 (the last value)" = "wrong_66",
  "64 (it wraps around)" = "wrong_64"
))
```


## Module 3: Data structures

- **vector** -- one sequence of values, all the same type
- **list** -- a sequence that *can* mix types
- **data frame** -- a table: rows are observations, columns are variables, and **each column is a vector**. `df$column_name` pulls one column out.

You'll work with data frames hands-on in Module 4.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
quiz_question_ui("structures_quiz", "A data frame called sites has columns name and temp. What is sites$temp?", c(
  "A vector of every value in the temp column" = "correct",
  "Just the first value in the temp column" = "wrong_one",
  "A one-row data frame" = "wrong_df",
  "The text \"temp\"" = "wrong_text"
))
```

## Module 3: Functions and comparisons

A few functions you'll see constantly: `sum(x)`, `mean(x)`, `round(x, digits)`.

**Comparisons** ask a yes/no question and give `TRUE` or `FALSE`: `==` (equal to), `!=` (not equal), `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`. On a vector, you get one answer per element -- and because R counts `TRUE` as 1, `sum()` of a comparison **counts** how many are true:

```{r comparison-demo, echo=TRUE}
c(5, 9, 2) > 4
sum(c(5, 9, 2) > 4)
```

The classic mistake: a single `=` *assigns* (like `<-`); only `==` *compares*.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
quiz_question_ui("comparison_quiz", "You want to check whether score is equal to 100, without changing its value. Which line does that?", c(
  "score = 100" = "wrong_assign1",
  "score == 100" = "correct",
  "score <- 100" = "wrong_assign2"
))
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
exercise_ui("fix_comparison_exercise", "temps <- c(72, 80, 85, 80, 79)\ntemps = 80\nsum(temps)")
```

## Module 3: Turning a formula into code

Work you're handed later often comes as a **formula**, not code. R's symbols match math closely: `+ - * /`, `^` for powers, `sqrt()` for square roots. The catch is **order of operations**: R does `^` first, then `*` and `/`, then `+` and `-` -- exactly like math class -- so parentheses matter. For example, Celsius to Fahrenheit:

$$
F = C \times \frac{9}{5} + 32
$$

```{r formula-demo, echo=TRUE}
celsius <- c(0, 20, 37)
celsius * 9 / 5 + 32
```

The fastest way to check formula code: **try it on a value you already know.** 0 °C should be 32 °F, and it is.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
quiz_question_ui("formula_quiz", "Which line computes the average of a and b?", c(
  "(a + b) / 2" = "correct",
  "a + b / 2" = "wrong_precedence",
  "mean(a, b)" = "wrong_mean"
))
```

### Practice: check the AI's conversion

An AI assistant wrote this to convert `temps_f` (Fahrenheit) to Celsius, using

$$
C = (F - 32) \times \frac{5}{9}
$$

It runs without an error. Check it against values you know (212 °F is 100 °C, and 32 °F is 0 °C), then fix it.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
exercise_ui("formula_exercise", "temps_f - 32 * 5 / 9")
```

## Module 3: Importing data

Real data lives in files, most often `.csv`, and you **import** it rather than typing it: `read.csv("file.csv")` reads one into a data frame (the tidyverse's `readr::read_csv()` does the same). The path is relative to your working directory (Module 1).

The first thing to do after importing is `str()`, to check that each column came in as the type you expect. A column of numbers with even **one** non-number in it -- `"n/a"`, `"-"`, `"<0.5"` -- arrives as text:

```
'data.frame':	4 obs. of  2 variables:
 $ site : chr  "A" "B" "C" "D"
 $ depth: chr  "1.2" "0.8" "n/a" "2.1"
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
quiz_question_ui("import_quiz", "In that str() output, why is depth chr (text) instead of num?", c(
  "One of its values, \"n/a\", isn't a number, so R read the whole column as text" = "correct",
  "read.csv() always imports every column as text" = "wrong_csv",
  "R can't store decimal numbers like 1.2" = "wrong_decimal",
  "The working directory was set wrong" = "wrong_wd"
))
```

## Module 3: Wrapping up

**If you remember only a few things from this module:**

- `<-` assigns, `==` compares -- and a single `=` assigns too.
- A variable holds a value, not a formula: change an input, and anything calculated from it must be recalculated.
- "It ran without an error" is not "it's right." Check results against something you already know.
- After importing, check column types with `str()` before trusting anything.

### Up next

Module 4 puts this to work on a real (messy) data frame.

```{r setup-module4, context="setup", include=FALSE}
library(dplyr)

# --- Practice data ---------------------------------------------------------
# A small, intentionally messy fish survey data set. Column names use the
# dot-separated, mixed-case style read.csv()/Excel exports commonly produce
# -- exactly what "Renaming columns" below has students fix. Two columns
# (Length.mm, Weight.g) include real NAs so later topics (NA handling,
# na.rm) have something genuine to work with, not a contrived edge case.
fish_survey <- data.frame(
  Fish.ID      = 1:10,
  Species.Name = c("Bluegill", "Bluegill", "Largemouth Bass", "Largemouth Bass",
                    "Yellow Perch", "Yellow Perch", "Bluegill", "Largemouth Bass",
                    "Yellow Perch", "Bluegill"),
  Length.mm    = c(152, 148, 310, NA, 205, 198, 160, 295, 210, 145),
  Weight.g     = c(45, 42, NA, 610, 98, 95, 50, 580, NA, 40),
  Lake.Site    = c("North Lake", "North Lake", "South Lake", "South Lake",
                    "North Lake", "South Lake", "North Lake", "South Lake",
                    "North Lake", "South Lake"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Already-renamed version, used by every exercise AFTER the renaming one --
# so later exercises don't depend on a student having gotten renaming right.
# Also reused as-is by Module 5 below (no need to rebuild it there now that
# both modules live in the same document/session).
fish_clean <- fish_survey
names(fish_clean) <- c("fish_id", "species", "length_mm", "weight_g", "lake_site")

# exercise_server() (R/tutor_utils.R) evaluates submitted code via
# eval(parse(text = user_code), envir = new.env()) -- new.env()'s parent
# chain resolves through wherever exercise_server() itself was source()'d
# (source()'s default local = FALSE means that's .GlobalEnv), NOT through
# this setup chunk's own local execution environment. Modules 1-3 never hit
# this because their exercises only ever built self-contained vectors from
# scratch -- this is the first module where exercise code needs to see a
# pre-existing shared object, so it needs to be explicitly placed in
# .GlobalEnv (safe here: both are static, read-only reference data, same
# for every session, set once when the R process starts).
assign("fish_survey", fish_survey, envir = globalenv())
assign("fish_clean", fish_clean, envir = globalenv())

# Grading logic for each exercise. log_attempt_and_maybe_open_chat() and
# wire_tutor_chat() themselves are shared across modules -- see
# R/tutor_utils.R.

evaluate_rename_exercise <- function(user_code, result, envir, stage) {
  expected_names <- c("fish_id", "species", "length_mm", "weight_g", "lake_site")
  has_fish_clean <- !is.null(envir) && exists("fish_clean", envir = envir, inherits = FALSE) &&
    is.data.frame(get("fish_clean", envir = envir))
  correct_result <- is.character(result) && identical(result, expected_names)

  passed <- has_fish_clean && correct_result

  feedback_message <- if (passed) {
    "All five columns are renamed correctly, in order -- fish_clean is ready to work with."
  } else if (identical(stage, "error_check")) {
    "That code doesn't run as-is -- check that every rename() argument has the form new_name = OldName, separated by commas."
  } else if (!has_fish_clean) {
    "fish_clean doesn't exist yet -- make sure the first line assigns the renamed result to fish_clean."
  } else {
    "fish_clean exists, but the column names aren't all correct yet -- check names(fish_clean) against fish_id, species, length_mm, weight_g, lake_site, in that order."
  }

  list(passed = passed, message = feedback_message)
}

evaluate_indexing_exercise <- function(user_code, result, stage) {
  uses_bracket <- grepl("\\[", user_code)
  uses_double_equals <- grepl("==", user_code, fixed = TRUE)
  correct_result <- is.data.frame(result) && nrow(result) == 5 && ncol(result) == 5 && all(result$lake_site == "North Lake")

  passed <- uses_bracket && correct_result

  feedback_message <- if (passed) {
    "Fixed -- 5 rows, all from North Lake, every column kept."
  } else if (identical(stage, "error_check") && !uses_double_equals) {
    "Still doesn't run. Inside a condition, = and == mean very different things -- which one compares two values?"
  } else if (identical(stage, "error_check")) {
    "The comparison looks right now, but R says it can't find those columns. Square brackets on a data frame take two parts -- what separates them, and which part is this condition for?"
  } else if (!uses_bracket) {
    "Keep using square-bracket indexing here (fish_clean[ ... ]), not a dplyr verb -- the point is to fix this code, not replace it."
  } else if ((is.data.frame(result) && ncol(result) != 5) || (!is.data.frame(result) && length(result) == 5)) {
    "The right rows, but not every column -- what goes after the comma decides the columns, and leaving it blank keeps them all."
  } else {
    "That runs, but it isn't returning exactly the 5 North Lake rows -- check the comparison (spelling and capitalization of \"North Lake\" matter)."
  }

  list(passed = passed, message = feedback_message)
}

evaluate_filter_select_exercise <- function(user_code, result, stage) {
  uses_filter <- grepl("filter\\s*\\(", user_code)
  uses_select <- grepl("select\\s*\\(", user_code)
  right_cols <- is.data.frame(result) && identical(names(result), c("species", "length_mm"))
  correct_result <- right_cols && nrow(result) == 2 && all(result$length_mm > 200)

  passed <- uses_filter && uses_select && correct_result

  feedback_message <- if (passed) {
    "Right -- just the two big South Lake fish (both Largemouth Bass). Notice the South Lake fish with a missing length didn't sneak in: filter() drops rows where the condition is NA."
  } else if (identical(stage, "error_check")) {
    "That code doesn't run as-is -- check that each condition compares with == or >, that text values are in quotes, and that each step is joined by |>."
  } else if (!uses_filter) {
    "This needs a filter() step to keep only the rows you want."
  } else if (!uses_select) {
    "This needs a select() step so only species and length_mm are left."
  } else if (!right_cols) {
    "The columns aren't right yet -- the result should have exactly species and length_mm, in that order."
  } else if (nrow(result) == 5) {
    "That's every South Lake fish, of any length -- filter() needs a second condition for length."
  } else if (nrow(result) == 4) {
    "Those are the long fish from BOTH lakes -- filter() also needs the lake condition."
  } else {
    "Not quite the right rows -- you should end up with exactly 2 fish. Check both conditions inside filter()."
  }

  list(passed = passed, message = feedback_message)
}

evaluate_mutate_arrange_exercise <- function(user_code, result, stage) {
  uses_mutate <- grepl("mutate\\s*\\(", user_code)
  uses_arrange <- grepl("arrange\\s*\\(", user_code)
  has_weight_kg <- is.data.frame(result) && "weight_kg" %in% names(result)
  correct_kg <- has_weight_kg && isTRUE(all.equal(result$weight_kg, result$weight_g / 1000))
  correct_order <- is.data.frame(result) && nrow(result) > 0 && isTRUE(result$length_mm[1] == 310)

  passed <- uses_mutate && uses_arrange && correct_kg && correct_order

  feedback_message <- if (passed) {
    "weight_kg is calculated correctly, and the rows are sorted with the longest fish first."
  } else if (identical(stage, "error_check")) {
    "That code doesn't run as-is -- check both mutate()'s and arrange()'s arguments are complete, valid R expressions, joined by |>."
  } else if (!uses_mutate || !has_weight_kg) {
    "mutate() should add a new column named exactly weight_kg."
  } else if (!correct_kg) {
    "weight_kg exists, but its values aren't the weight in kilograms yet -- how many grams are in a kilogram?"
  } else if (!uses_arrange || !correct_order) {
    "weight_kg looks right, but the longest fish isn't first yet -- arrange() sorts smallest-first unless you tell it otherwise."
  } else {
    "Almost there -- double check both the mutate() and arrange() steps."
  }

  list(passed = passed, message = feedback_message)
}

evaluate_group_summarize_exercise <- function(user_code, result, stage) {
  uses_group_by <- grepl("group_by\\s*\\(", user_code)
  uses_summarize <- grepl("summari[sz]e\\s*\\(", user_code)
  has_cols <- is.data.frame(result) && all(c("max_weight", "n_fish") %in% names(result))
  right_shape <- is.data.frame(result) && nrow(result) == 3 && "species" %in% names(result)
  right_counts <- has_cols && right_shape &&
    identical(as.integer(result$n_fish[order(result$species)]), c(4L, 3L, 3L))
  no_na <- has_cols && right_shape && !any(is.na(result$max_weight))
  right_values <- no_na && isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(result$max_weight[order(result$species)]), c(50, 610, 98)))

  passed <- uses_group_by && uses_summarize && has_cols && right_shape && right_counts && right_values

  feedback_message <- if (passed) {
    "Three species, each with its heaviest weight and a fish count -- exactly right. (Notice n_fish still counts every fish, including the ones whose weight is missing.)"
  } else if (identical(stage, "error_check")) {
    "That code doesn't run as-is -- check that group_by() and summarize() are joined by |>, and that summarize()'s two results are separated by a comma."
  } else if (!uses_group_by || !right_shape) {
    "You should get one row per species (3 rows) -- check what you're grouping by."
  } else if (!has_cols) {
    "summarize() should create two columns, named exactly max_weight and n_fish."
  } else if (!right_counts) {
    "n_fish isn't counting the fish in each group correctly yet -- the demo above shows the function that counts rows per group."
  } else if (!no_na) {
    "Look at the printed result: some species' max_weight is NA. What's different about those species' data, and how do you tell max() to cope with it?"
  } else if (!right_values) {
    "max_weight should be each species' single heaviest fish -- check that you're using max() on weight_g."
  } else {
    "Close -- double check both steps."
  }

  list(passed = passed, message = feedback_message)
}

evaluate_na_handling_exercise <- function(user_code, result, stage) {
  uses_filter <- grepl("filter\\s*\\(", user_code)
  uses_is_na <- grepl("is\\.na\\s*\\(", user_code)
  uses_na_rm <- grepl("na\\.rm", user_code)
  has_col <- is.data.frame(result) && "avg_weight" %in% names(result) && "species" %in% names(result) && nrow(result) == 3
  correct_result <- has_col &&
    isTRUE(all.equal(result$avg_weight[order(result$species)], c(44.25, 595, 96.5)))

  passed <- uses_filter && uses_is_na && correct_result

  feedback_message <- if (passed) {
    "Fixed -- every species has a real average now, with the two fish of unknown weight left out before averaging."
  } else if (identical(stage, "error_check")) {
    "That code doesn't run as-is -- check that the new filter() step is joined with |> and that ! and is.na(...) are written correctly."
  } else if (uses_na_rm && !uses_filter) {
    "na.rm = TRUE would fix the NA too -- but this exercise is about the other approach: removing the incomplete rows with filter() before averaging."
  } else if (!uses_filter || !uses_is_na) {
    "Add a filter() step that keeps only rows where weight_g is NOT missing -- is.na() finds missing values, and ! flips TRUE/FALSE."
  } else if (has_col && any(is.na(result$avg_weight))) {
    "Still NA -- check the filter() keeps the rows that are NOT missing (and that it runs before summarize())."
  } else if (!has_col) {
    "The result should still have one row per species with an avg_weight column -- keep the original group_by() and summarize() steps."
  } else {
    "That's filtering something, but the averages aren't right yet -- double check the condition inside filter()."
  }

  list(passed = passed, message = feedback_message)
}

evaluate_module4_cumulative_exercise <- function(user_code, result, stage) {
  uses_filter <- grepl("filter\\s*\\(", user_code)
  uses_group_by <- grepl("group_by\\s*\\(", user_code)
  uses_arrange <- grepl("arrange\\s*\\(", user_code)
  is_df <- is.data.frame(result) && "avg_length" %in% names(result)
  by_lake <- is_df && "lake_site" %in% names(result)
  right_shape <- by_lake && nrow(result) == 2
  no_na <- is_df && nrow(result) > 0 && !any(is.na(result$avg_length))
  right_order <- right_shape && identical(as.character(result$lake_site[1]), "South Lake")

  passed <- uses_filter && uses_group_by && uses_arrange && right_shape && no_na && right_order

  feedback_message <- if (passed) {
    "All three bugs fixed -- missing lengths dropped, averaged per lake, highest first (South Lake, 237 mm)."
  } else if (identical(stage, "error_check")) {
    "That code doesn't run as-is now -- work through it one pipe step at a time (try running just the first line or two to see what each produces)."
  } else if (!is_df || !uses_filter || !uses_group_by || !uses_arrange) {
    "Keep all four steps (filter, group_by, summarize, arrange) -- each has a bug to fix, but none should be removed."
  } else if (!no_na || nrow(result) < 2) {
    "Look at what the filter() step keeps: is.na(length_mm) is TRUE for the rows that ARE missing. Is that what you want to keep?"
  } else if (!by_lake || !right_shape) {
    "The goal is one average per LAKE -- check what the data is being grouped by."
  } else if (!right_order) {
    "The averages are right, but the lowest one is first -- the goal asks for the highest average first."
  } else {
    "Close -- double check each step against the goal."
  }

  list(passed = passed, message = feedback_message)
}
```

```{r, context="server"}
# --- Quiz question wiring ------------------------------------------------
# Module 4's quizzes are deliberately "predict the result" questions, not
# definition recall -- each answer has to be reasoned out from the data or
# the code shown, and every wrong option is a specific, common mistake.
quiz_question_server(input, output, session, "inspect_quiz", module_number = 4, list(
  wrong_vector = list(correct = FALSE, message = "Close -- that gives one TRUE/FALSE per fish. You'd still have to count the TRUEs. What adds them up?"),
  correct = list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct! is.na() marks each missing value TRUE, and sum() counts TRUEs (TRUE counts as 1). There are 2."),
  wrong_length = list(correct = FALSE, message = "length() counts every value in the column, missing or not -- that's 10."),
  wrong_dims = list(correct = FALSE, message = "That's just rows minus columns (10 - 5) -- it doesn't look at the values at all.")
))

quiz_question_server(input, output, session, "indexing_quiz", module_number = 4, list(
  correct = list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct! Row 2, column \"species\" -- a single value."),
  wrong_column = list(correct = FALSE, message = "That would be fish_clean[, \"species\"] -- with the row part left blank. Here the row part is 2."),
  wrong_row = list(correct = FALSE, message = "That would be fish_clean[2, ] -- with the column part left blank. Here the column part is \"species\"."),
  wrong_error = list(correct = FALSE, message = "Mixing a row number and a column name is fine -- each side of the comma is handled separately.")
))

quiz_question_server(input, output, session, "pipe_quiz", module_number = 4, list(
  correct = list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct! sqrt() runs first, giving 2, 3, 4 -- then sum() adds those up to 9."),
  wrong_order = list(correct = FALSE, message = "That's sqrt(sum(...)) -- the steps in the other order. The pipe runs left to right: sqrt first, then sum."),
  wrong_nosqrt = list(correct = FALSE, message = "That's the sum without the square roots -- but sqrt() runs first here."),
  wrong_vector = list(correct = FALSE, message = "That's what you'd have after sqrt() -- but there's one more step after it.")
))

quiz_question_server(input, output, session, "arrange_na_quiz", module_number = 4, list(
  correct = list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct! arrange() always puts NA at the very end -- even with desc(). Worth remembering when \"the last row\" looks odd."),
  wrong_first = list(correct = FALSE, message = "desc() flips the order of the real values, but NA isn't a value it can rank -- it always goes last."),
  wrong_dropped = list(correct = FALSE, message = "arrange() only reorders rows -- it never removes any. (filter() is the one that drops rows.)"),
  wrong_error = list(correct = FALSE, message = "No error -- arrange() handles missing values fine; it just has a fixed place to put them.")
))

quiz_question_server(input, output, session, "group_count_quiz", module_number = 4, list(
  correct = list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct! One row per species/lake combination that actually appears in the data -- and there are 5 of them."),
  wrong_all_combos = list(correct = FALSE, message = "3 species x 2 lakes is 6 possible combinations -- but Largemouth Bass only shows up in South Lake, so only 5 actually occur."),
  wrong_species_only = list(correct = FALSE, message = "That's what group_by(species) alone would give. Grouping by two columns splits each species further by lake."),
  wrong_rows = list(correct = FALSE, message = "summarize() collapses each group down to ONE row -- so the result has one row per group, not one per fish.")
))

quiz_question_server(input, output, session, "na_quiz", module_number = 4, list(
  wrong_20 = list(correct = FALSE, message = "R doesn't just skip the NA silently -- it has to be told to."),
  correct = list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct! Any arithmetic involving NA returns NA by default, unless you tell R how to handle it."),
  wrong_40 = list(correct = FALSE, message = "R doesn't treat a missing value as 0 -- it treats the whole result as unknown (NA).")
))

quiz_question_server(input, output, session, "bracket_na_quiz", module_number = 4, list(
  wrong_4 = list(correct = FALSE, message = "That's what filter(length_mm > 200) would give -- filter() drops rows where the condition is NA. Square brackets don't."),
  correct = list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct -- and it's a sneaky one. 4 fish are over 200 mm, but the fish with a missing length gives NA instead of TRUE/FALSE, and square brackets return a row of all NAs for it. filter() would give 4."),
  wrong_9 = list(correct = FALSE, message = "Only 4 fish are actually longer than 200 mm -- the question is what happens to the one with a missing length."),
  wrong_error = list(correct = FALSE, message = "No error -- R runs this happily. That's what makes it dangerous: the result quietly includes a row you didn't ask for.")
))
```

## Module 4: Welcome back

This module is where you start **working with a real data frame**: inspecting it, cleaning it, and asking it questions with `dplyr`. The exercises get harder as you go and lean less and less on fill-in-the-blanks -- by the end you'll be fixing broken code someone else wrote, which is most of what working with R actually looks like.

When you get stuck, open **Ask the Tutor** under the exercise -- before submitting, after a miss, or after passing. It sees your latest attempt and will help you get there without just handing you the answer.

The data is `fish_survey`, from a (fictional) survey of two lakes. Notice the awkward column names and the missing values (`NA`) -- dealing with both is what this module is about.

```{r fish-survey-demo, echo=TRUE}
fish_survey
```

## Module 4: Inspecting a data frame

Look before you change anything:

- **`str(x)`** -- each column's name, type, and first few values
- **`head(x)`** -- the first few rows
- **`nrow(x)` / `ncol(x)`** -- the number of rows / columns
- **`names(x)`** -- the column names
- **`summary(x)`** -- min, max, mean, and how many values are missing, per column

```{r inspect-demo, echo=TRUE}
str(fish_survey)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
quiz_question_ui("inspect_quiz", "Which line tells you how many fish have a missing weight?", c(
  "is.na(fish_survey$Weight.g)" = "wrong_vector",
  "sum(is.na(fish_survey$Weight.g))" = "correct",
  "length(fish_survey$Weight.g)" = "wrong_length",
  "nrow(fish_survey) - ncol(fish_survey)" = "wrong_dims"
))
```

## Module 4: Renaming columns

Imported data often arrives with names like `Species.Name`. `rename()` fixes them, always written `new_name = OldName`:

```{r rename-demo, echo=TRUE}
fish_survey |> rename(species = Species.Name) |> names()
```

## Module 4: Indexing and subsetting

From here on, everything uses `fish_clean` -- an already-renamed copy, so nothing depends on your rename answer.

Base R pulls out rows and columns with square brackets: `df[rows, columns]`. Leave a side blank to keep all of it, and use a condition in place of row numbers to keep only matching rows:

```{r indexing-demo, echo=TRUE}
fish_clean[1, ]
fish_clean[fish_clean$species == "Bluegill", c("species", "length_mm")]
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
  "The whole species column" = "wrong_column",
  "Row 2, with every column" = "wrong_row",
  "An error -- you can't mix a row number and a column name" = "wrong_error"
))
```

## Module 4: The pipe operator

The pipe, `|>`, passes the value on its left in as the first argument of the function on its right: `x |> mean()` is the same as `mean(x)`. Chains read left to right, as "then":

```{r pipe-demo, echo=TRUE}
fish_clean$length_mm |> mean(na.rm = TRUE)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
quiz_question_ui("pipe_quiz", "What does c(4, 9, 16) |> sqrt() |> sum() return?", c(
  "9" = "correct",
  "5.39 (the square root of 29)" = "wrong_order",
  "29" = "wrong_nosqrt",
  "c(2, 3, 4)" = "wrong_vector"
))
```

## Module 4: Filtering and selecting

- **`filter()`** keeps the rows that match a condition. Give it several conditions separated by commas, and a row has to meet **all** of them.
- **`select()`** keeps only the columns you name.

```{r filter-select-demo, echo=TRUE}
fish_clean |>
  filter(species == "Bluegill", length_mm < 150) |>
  select(fish_id, lake_site)
```

## Module 4: Adding columns and sorting

- **`mutate(new_col = ...)`** adds a column calculated from existing ones.
- **`arrange(col)`** sorts rows smallest-first; **`arrange(desc(col))`** sorts largest-first.

```{r mutate-arrange-demo, echo=TRUE}
fish_clean |>
  mutate(length_cm = length_mm / 10) |>
  arrange(desc(weight_g))
```

## Module 4: Grouping and summarizing

`group_by()` splits the rows into groups, and `summarize()` collapses each group to a single row. `summarize()` can compute several things at once, separated by commas -- and `n()` counts the rows in each group:

```{r group-summarize-demo, echo=TRUE}
fish_clean |>
  group_by(lake_site) |>
  summarize(n_fish = n(), shortest = min(length_mm, na.rm = TRUE))
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
quiz_question_ui("group_count_quiz", "How many rows does fish_clean |> group_by(species, lake_site) |> summarize(n = n()) return? (Scroll up to the data if you need to.)", c(
  "3" = "wrong_species_only",
  "5" = "correct",
  "6" = "wrong_all_combos",
  "10" = "wrong_rows"
))
```

## Module 4: Handling missing data

```{r, echo=FALSE}
quiz_question_ui("na_quiz", "What does mean(c(10, NA, 30)) return, without any extra arguments?", c(
  "20" = "wrong_20",
  "NA" = "correct",
  "40" = "wrong_40"
))
```

There are two ways to deal with `NA`: tell the function to skip it (`na.rm = TRUE`), or remove the incomplete rows first. `is.na(x)` is `TRUE` wherever `x` is missing and `!` means "not", so `filter(!is.na(x))` keeps only complete rows:

```{r na-demo, echo=TRUE}
fish_clean |> filter(!is.na(weight_g))
```

Missing values can also sneak *into* results. Look closely at the data before answering this one:

```{r, echo=FALSE}
quiz_question_ui("bracket_na_quiz", "How many rows does fish_clean[fish_clean$length_mm > 200, ] return?", c(
  "4" = "wrong_4",
  "5" = "correct",
  "9" = "wrong_9",
  "An error" = "wrong_error"
))
```

This code should give the average weight of each species, but two of the three come out `NA`. Fix it by **removing the incomplete rows with `filter()`** before averaging (not with `na.rm`).

## Module 4: Wrapping up

**If you remember only a few things from this module:**

- The pipe (`|>`) reads as "then" -- and when a pipeline gives a wrong answer, check it one step at a time against what each step is supposed to do.
- `group_by()` + `summarize()` takes you from many rows to one answer per group -- one of the most common things you'll do with real data.
- Missing values (`NA`) don't disappear on their own: `mean()` returns `NA` unless told otherwise, `arrange()` sends them to the bottom, and square-bracket subsetting can quietly add rows of them.

### Up next

Module 5 moves into actually *doing something* with cleaned-up data: basic plots with `ggplot2`, and a light-touch introduction to a few habits (script organization, file naming, and version control awareness) that carry into real work beyond this course.

```{r setup-module5, context="setup", include=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(rlang)

# Module 5 reuses the fish_clean data frame Module 4 built and placed in
# globalenv() above.

# A ggplot object's mapping (aes()) is stored as quosures --
# rlang::as_label() turns e.g. aes(x = length_mm)'s stored mapping back into
# the plain string "length_mm" for comparison. A mapping can live on the
# ggplot() call or on a layer (geom_point(aes(...))), so plot_mapping_label()
# checks both.
mapping_label <- function(mapping, aesthetic) {
  if (is.null(mapping[[aesthetic]])) return(NA_character_)
  rlang::as_label(mapping[[aesthetic]])
}

plot_mapping_label <- function(plot, aesthetic) {
  label <- mapping_label(plot$mapping, aesthetic)
  if (!is.na(label)) return(label)
  for (layer in plot$layers) {
    label <- mapping_label(layer$mapping, aesthetic)
    if (!is.na(label)) return(label)
  }
  NA_character_
}

evaluate_scatter_exercise <- function(user_code, result, stage) {
  is_ggplot <- inherits(result, "ggplot")
  has_point_layer <- is_ggplot && any(vapply(result$layers, function(l) inherits(l$geom, "GeomPoint"), logical(1)))
  x_ok <- is_ggplot && identical(plot_mapping_label(result, "x"), "length_mm")
  y_ok <- is_ggplot && identical(plot_mapping_label(result, "y"), "weight_g")
  colour_label <- if (is_ggplot) plot_mapping_label(result, "colour") else NA_character_
  colour_ok <- identical(colour_label, "species")

  passed <- is_ggplot && has_point_layer && x_ok && y_ok && colour_ok

  feedback_message <- if (passed) {
    "That's it -- one color per species, with a legend ggplot made for you, because color is mapped to a column inside aes()."
  } else if (identical(stage, "error_check") && grepl("species", user_code, fixed = TRUE)) {
    "R can't find an object called species. Outside aes(), R looks for a variable by that name; inside aes(), it looks for a column in the data. Where does color = species belong?"
  } else if (identical(stage, "error_check")) {
    "That code doesn't run as-is -- check that every ( has a matching ) and the layers are joined with +."
  } else if (!is_ggplot || !has_point_layer) {
    "Keep the ggplot(...) + geom_point() structure -- you only need to add one thing to it."
  } else if (!x_ok || !y_ok) {
    "Keep length_mm on x and weight_g on y -- only the color should change."
  } else if (identical(colour_label, "\"species\"")) {
    "Close -- but \"species\" in quotes is just a piece of text, so every point gets the same color. Drop the quotes so it refers to the column."
  } else {
    "The points should be colored by species -- map color to the species column inside aes()."
  }

  list(passed = passed, message = feedback_message)
}

evaluate_bar_exercise <- function(user_code, result, stage) {
  uses_group_by <- grepl("group_by\\s*\\(", user_code)
  is_ggplot <- inherits(result, "ggplot")
  has_col_layer <- is_ggplot && any(vapply(result$layers, function(l) inherits(l$geom, "GeomCol"), logical(1)))
  has_count_bar <- is_ggplot && any(vapply(result$layers, function(l) inherits(l$stat, "StatCount"), logical(1)))
  right_groups <- is_ggplot && is.data.frame(result$data) && nrow(result$data) == 3
  x_ok <- is_ggplot && identical(plot_mapping_label(result, "x"), "species")
  y_ok <- is_ggplot && identical(plot_mapping_label(result, "y"), "mean_weight")

  passed <- uses_group_by && is_ggplot && has_col_layer && right_groups && x_ok && y_ok

  feedback_message <- if (passed) {
    "Fixed -- now each bar's height is that species' mean weight instead of a count of rows."
  } else if (identical(stage, "error_check") && grepl("geom_bar", user_code, fixed = TRUE)) {
    "geom_bar() won't take a y value -- it always counts rows itself (that's what stat_count() in the error means). Which geom draws bars at heights you already have?"
  } else if (identical(stage, "error_check")) {
    "That code doesn't run as-is -- work through each step of the pipeline, same as Module 4."
  } else if (!uses_group_by || !right_groups) {
    "Keep the group_by() and summarize() steps -- there should be one bar per species (3 bars)."
  } else if (has_count_bar && y_ok) {
    "Half right -- the y mapping is good, but geom_bar() won't accept a y value (that's the stat_count() error above the plot). It always counts rows itself. Which geom draws bars at heights you already have?"
  } else if (has_count_bar || !has_col_layer) {
    "Every bar is still height 1. geom_bar() counts how many rows each species has -- and after summarize() there's exactly one. You want the bar height to come from mean_weight."
  } else if (!x_ok) {
    "Keep species on the x-axis."
  } else {
    "Close -- the bar heights should come from mean_weight. Check aes()."
  }

  list(passed = passed, message = feedback_message)
}

evaluate_histogram_exercise <- function(user_code, result, stage) {
  is_ggplot <- inherits(result, "ggplot")
  hist_layers <- if (is_ggplot) Filter(function(l) inherits(l$stat, "StatBin"), result$layers) else list()
  has_hist_layer <- length(hist_layers) > 0
  x_ok <- is_ggplot && identical(plot_mapping_label(result, "x"), "length_mm")
  bins_ok <- has_hist_layer && isTRUE(hist_layers[[1]]$stat_params$bins == 8)

  passed <- is_ggplot && has_hist_layer && x_ok && bins_ok

  feedback_message <- if (passed) {
    "That's a histogram of length_mm with 8 bins. (ggplot warns that 1 row was removed -- that's the fish with a missing length.)"
  } else if (identical(stage, "error_check")) {
    "That code doesn't run as-is -- check that aes() has x = a column name and that the parentheses all match."
  } else if (!is_ggplot) {
    "This should produce a ggplot object -- keep ggplot(fish_clean, aes(...)) at the start."
  } else if (!has_hist_layer) {
    "This needs a geom_histogram() layer to draw the histogram."
  } else if (!x_ok) {
    "The x-axis should be length_mm -- check aes()."
  } else {
    "Almost -- the histogram should use exactly 8 bins. Look at how the demo sets the number of bins."
  }

  list(passed = passed, message = feedback_message)
}

evaluate_cumulative_plot_exercise <- function(user_code, result, stage) {
  is_ggplot <- inherits(result, "ggplot")
  has_point_layer <- is_ggplot && any(vapply(result$layers, function(l) inherits(l$geom, "GeomPoint"), logical(1)))
  n_rows <- if (is_ggplot && is.data.frame(result$data)) nrow(result$data) else NA_integer_
  right_data <- is_ggplot && isTRUE(n_rows == 4) && all(result$data$species == "Bluegill")
  has_title <- is_ggplot && is.character(result$labels$title) && nzchar(trimws(result$labels$title))

  passed <- is_ggplot && has_point_layer && right_data && has_title

  feedback_message <- if (passed) {
    "Both bugs fixed -- 4 Bluegill, plotted and titled. The second bug was the dangerous one: an empty plot runs without any error."
  } else if (identical(stage, "error_check")) {
    "Read the error closely -- ggplot is making a specific guess about what's wrong. ggplot layers are joined with + , not the pipe."
  } else if (!is_ggplot || !has_point_layer) {
    "Keep the ggplot(...) + geom_point() + labs(...) structure."
  } else if (isTRUE(n_rows == 0)) {
    "It runs now -- but look at the plot: there are no points. filter() kept zero rows. Compare the species name in the code to how it's written in the data."
  } else if (!right_data) {
    "The plot should show only the 4 Bluegill -- check the filter() step."
  } else {
    "Keep the title -- the plot should still have labs(title = ...)."
  }

  list(passed = passed, message = feedback_message)
}
```

## Module 5: Welcome back

This module turns `fish_clean` into plots with `ggplot2`. You'll mostly **adjust and fix** plotting code rather than write it from a blank page -- which is how plotting code usually gets used, whether it comes from a colleague, an old script, or an AI. The module ends with a few working habits that keep code runnable on someone else's computer.

## Module 5: Basic plots with ggplot2

Every `ggplot2` plot has the same shape:

- **`ggplot(data, aes(...))`** starts the plot. `aes()` ("aesthetics") **maps columns to visual properties**: which column goes on x, which on y, which sets the color.
- **`+ geom_...()`** adds a layer that draws something: `geom_point()` for points, `geom_col()` for bars, `geom_histogram()` for a distribution.

Layers are joined with `+`, not the pipe.

```{r ggplot-demo, echo=TRUE, fig.height=3}
ggplot(fish_clean, aes(x = species, y = length_mm)) +
  geom_point()
```

**Inside `aes()`** means "take this from a column in the data." **Outside `aes()`** means "use this fixed value for everything": `geom_point(color = "blue")` makes every point blue.

<details>
<summary><strong>New to plotting code?</strong> How to read a ggplot line.</summary>

Read it left to right as a sentence: "Using `fish_clean`, put `species` on the x-axis and `length_mm` on the y-axis, then draw points." Each `+` adds one more instruction -- another layer, a title, a color scale. You can delete a layer and the rest still works, which makes ggplot code easy to take apart when something looks wrong.

</details>

```{r, echo=FALSE}
quiz_question_ui("ggplot_grammar_quiz", "What does ggplot(fish_clean, aes(x = length_mm, y = weight_g)) + geom_point(aes(color = \"blue\")) draw?", c(
  "Points in ggplot's default reddish color, with a legend labeled \"blue\"" = "correct",
  "Blue points, with no legend" = "wrong_blue",
  "An error" = "wrong_error",
  "An empty plot with no points" = "wrong_none"
))
```

## Module 5: Bar charts from summarized data

Bar charts usually show *summarized* data -- exactly what `group_by()` + `summarize()` produce -- and you can pipe a summary straight into `ggplot()`. There are two bar geoms, and mixing them up is a common silent mistake:

- **`geom_col()`** draws each bar at the height of a **y value you already have**.
- **`geom_bar()`** **counts rows** itself and draws that count -- no y needed.

```{r bar-demo, echo=TRUE, fig.height=3}
fish_clean |>
  group_by(lake_site) |>
  summarize(mean_length = mean(length_mm, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = lake_site, y = mean_length)) +
  geom_col()
```

## Module 5: Histograms

A histogram shows how one numeric column is **distributed**: it splits the values into bins and counts how many fall in each. `bins` sets how many.

```{r histogram-demo, echo=TRUE, fig.height=3}
ggplot(fish_clean, aes(x = weight_g)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 6)
```

Running that in RStudio also prints: `Removed 2 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range (stat_bin())`.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
  "The plot is wrong and needs to be redone" = "wrong_wrong",
  "Two of the bins were empty" = "wrong_bins",
  "2 rows were deleted from fish_clean" = "wrong_deleted"
))
```
